name: Maximum Entropy Reinforcement Learning (MaxEnt RL)
key_paper: Ziebart, B. D., Bagnell, J. A., & Dey, A. K. (2010). Modeling Interaction via the Principle of Maximum Causal Entropy. ICML 2010. Extended by: Haarnoja, T., Tang, H., Abbeel, P., & Levine, S. (2017). Reinforcement Learning with Deep Energy-Based Policies. ICML 2017. Consolidated in: Haarnoja, T., Zhou, A., Abbeel, P., & Levine, S. (2018). Soft Actor-Critic: Off-Policy Maximum Entropy Deep Reinforcement Learning with a Stochastic Actor. ICML 2018.
algorithm_description: Maximum Entropy RL augments the standard RL objective (maximize expected cumulative reward) with an entropy regularization term H(pi) that penalizes low-entropy, near-deterministic policies. The combined objective is J(pi) = E[sum_t (r_t + alpha * H(pi(.|s_t)))], where alpha is a temperature coefficient controlling the exploration-exploitation tradeoff. The entropy term prevents the policy from collapsing onto a single action or a narrow set of actions even when one action dominates in expected reward. In the discrete setting, H(pi) = -sum_a pi(a|s) * log pi(a|s), which is maximized by a uniform distribution. Policy gradient updates include an additional term proportional to -log pi(a|s) (the score of the sampled action), which acts as a built-in diversity reward at every update step. The framework subsumes temperature-scaled softmax sampling as a special case: at convergence the optimal MaxEnt policy is pi*(a|s) proportional to exp(Q*(s,a) / alpha), which is exactly a softmax over Q-values.
action_space_handling: MaxEnt RL is defined for any action space where a probability distribution can be parameterized and its entropy computed. For flat discrete action spaces (finite |A|), the policy is a categorical distribution and entropy is the standard Shannon entropy. For combinatorial action spaces (select k from N), the technique must be adapted: (1) factored autoregressive: apply entropy bonus independently at each of the k autoregressive steps, summing H(pi_t) across steps t=1..k; (2) joint combinatorial: directly parameterize a distribution over k-subsets and compute subset entropy -- tractable only for small N; (3) energy-based: treat the policy as an unnormalized energy function over subsets and use contrastive divergence or MCMC estimation of entropy. The autoregressive factored approach is the standard practical choice for N=50, k=7.
how_combinatorial_output_is_formed: In the lottery-nn context, combinatorial output (7 distinct numbers from 1-50) is formed via autoregressive masked sampling with per-step entropy bonuses. At each step t=1..7, the policy network outputs a logit vector of length 50; previously selected numbers are masked to -inf; a softmax is applied over the remaining candidates; one number is sampled. The entropy of each step's masked softmax is computed and added to the entropy bonus for that transition. Alternatively, MaxEnt RL can be applied as a post-hoc modification to the existing temperature-softmax predict.py: replace the fixed temperature with a learned, reward-conditioned temperature, or add an explicit entropy reward term -alpha * log(pi(a)) to each step reward before computing policy gradients via REINFORCE.
sequential_generation_strategy: Autoregressive (one number at a time, conditioned on the set already selected). MaxEnt RL is agnostic to the generation strategy -- it adds an entropy term on top of whatever policy distribution is used. If the lottery-nn uses a flat multi-hot output head, MaxEnt applies to the joint distribution over all 50 logits simultaneously (treating the multi-hot mask as a Bernoulli product distribution). If autoregressive masking is used, MaxEnt applies step-by-step. The autoregressive approach is preferred because it allows inter-number correlations to be modeled (each step is conditioned on prior selections) and the entropy bonus can be applied at granular per-number resolution rather than the entire set at once.
gradient_estimator_type: For on-policy MaxEnt RL: REINFORCE (score function estimator) with the entropy bonus gradient -log pi(a|s) added analytically. The entropy gradient is exact (no sampling required) because H(pi) = -E[log pi(a)] and d/d_theta H(pi) = -E[(1 + log pi(a)) * d/d_theta log pi(a)]. This means the entropy gradient adds negligible variance compared to the reward-only REINFORCE gradient. For off-policy MaxEnt RL (SAC): the Actor is updated via a reparameterized or closed-form expected Q-value gradient, with entropy computed exactly from the softmax distribution. No Gumbel-softmax or straight-through estimator is needed. Overall, MaxEnt RL is gradient-estimator-friendly: the entropy bonus is always differentiable with respect to policy parameters, regardless of whether the reward gradient uses REINFORCE or reparameterization.
combinatorial_constraint_enforcement: Autoregressive masking enforces the k-distinct constraint: after selecting number i, its logit is set to -inf before the softmax at the next step, making reselection probability exactly zero. This is compatible with the entropy bonus because the entropy is computed over the masked softmax distribution (only over remaining candidates), not the full 50-dimensional vector. The MaxEnt objective naturally discourages the policy from concentrating probability mass on a single candidate at each step, which means the masking constraint and the entropy objective work in the same direction -- both push the policy to spread probability mass across the remaining pool.
sample_efficiency_rating: Medium. MaxEnt RL as a standalone technique does not improve sample efficiency beyond the base policy gradient or actor-critic algorithm it is applied to. Its benefit is qualitative: it prevents mode collapse (the primary failure mode with small n), which indirectly helps because a diverse policy explores more of the action space and thus gathers more informative signal per draw. With fewer than 200 training samples (draws), the entropy bonus is crucial because it keeps the policy from premature convergence to a memorized pattern. However, convergence of the Q-function or value baseline (if used) is still limited by data quantity. Rated medium rather than high because the sparse reward signal (~95% zero-hit plays) limits learning even with good entropy regularization.
regularization_built_in: Entropy bonus is the core built-in regularization: the policy is penalized for low entropy at every update, preventing collapse to a deterministic subset of numbers. The temperature coefficient alpha controls regularization strength -- high alpha forces high entropy (near-uniform play generation), low alpha allows exploitation of learned Q-values. Automatic alpha tuning (dual-gradient descent targeting a minimum entropy threshold) is available in SAC-style implementations. No dropout or weight decay is intrinsic to MaxEnt RL itself, but they can be freely combined. KL-regularized variants (penalizing KL divergence from a reference policy rather than raw entropy) are also common and add an additional anchor against deviation from prior behavior.
known_failure_modes_on_small_data: Entropy over-regularization: if alpha is set too high, the policy remains near-uniform regardless of reward signal, effectively ignoring what little the model has learned from 100-200 draws. Alpha needs careful manual tuning or automatic scheduling with small datasets. Entropy plateau: with very sparse rewards, the entropy bonus dominates the gradient and the policy optimizes for entropy rather than reward, producing diverse plays with no hit-rate improvement over random. Value function noise: if MaxEnt RL is used with a critic (SAC), Q-function bootstrapping on fewer than 200 transitions can be noisy, causing instability in the temperature-adjusted Q targets. Log-probability overflow: computing log pi(a) for near-zero probabilities can cause numerical instability unless logits are clamped.
data_regime_evidence: Ziebart et al. (2010) validated MaxEnt inverse RL on trajectory datasets of 100-500 demonstrations, which is structurally comparable to 100-200 draw history. The entropy regularization was effective at preventing overfitting to the small demonstration set. Haarnoja et al. (2017, 2018) validated SAC (which embeds MaxEnt RL) on continuous control benchmarks with thousands of environment steps -- not the small-data regime. Direct empirical validation of MaxEnt RL with fewer than 200 discrete combinatorial training samples has not been published as a standalone study. minimum_training_samples_tested: [uncertain] -- the MaxEnt IRL literature suggests effective use around 100-500 demonstrations, but this is inverse RL (imitation), not forward RL with sparse reward. performance_degradation_curve: [uncertain]. comparison_baseline: [uncertain] for the lottery-specific setting.
convergence_guarantees_small_n: For tabular MDPs, MaxEnt RL has well-defined optimal solutions: the soft Bellman equations have a unique fixed point and policy gradient ascent on the MaxEnt objective converges to this fixed point under standard conditions (Ziebart 2010, Haarnoja 2017). These guarantees are asymptotic and do not provide finite-sample rates for n < 200. With deep function approximators, no finite-sample convergence bounds exist. Empirically, the entropy bonus stabilizes training compared to pure reward-seeking objectives (less divergence, more consistent hit rates), but this is anecdotal rather than formally proven for small n. The most relevant guarantee is that the MaxEnt optimal policy is strictly stochastic (non-degenerate) by construction, which rules out the worst failure mode (complete mode collapse) even at convergence.
reward_distribution_handling: MaxEnt RL does not directly address reward sparsity -- it adds entropy to the objective but does not reshape the reward distribution. However, the entropy bonus -alpha * log pi(a|s) acts as a dense pseudo-reward at every action step, providing a non-zero gradient signal even when the draw reward is zero. This is critical for the lottery domain where ~95% of plays score 0 hits. The effective reward becomes r_t + alpha * H(pi_t), which is always non-zero when entropy is non-zero. The lottery reward distribution (0 for no hit, 1-7 for hits) is handled by the underlying policy gradient or actor-critic algorithm; MaxEnt RL does not need distributional return modeling. Minimum draws needed for stable learning: approximately 50-100 draws are sufficient to avoid complete gradient collapse, with alpha providing the floor of gradient signal.
credit_assignment_granularity: MaxEnt RL assigns entropy credit at the action-generation step level: each of the k autoregressive steps receives an entropy bonus proportional to -alpha * log pi(number_t | selected_so_far). This is number-level credit, not just play-level credit. The draw reward (number of hits) is assigned at play level unless explicitly shaped. Combining number-level entropy credit with number-level reward shaping (semi-bandit feedback: reward +1 for each number that appears in the draw) gives the finest-grained credit assignment possible and is the recommended approach for lottery-nn. The entropy bonus alone is not a substitute for number-level reward -- it incentivizes diversity, not accuracy.
diversity_mechanism: The entropy bonus is the direct diversity mechanism. Maximizing H(pi) penalizes the policy for concentrating probability mass on any single number or small subset of numbers, forcing the softmax distribution to remain spread out across candidates at each generation step. This directly prevents the known failure mode of temperature-softmax generation (repeated identical plays when temperature is too low). Across multiple plays generated in a single predict call, diversity is achieved by sampling from the stochastic policy independently for each play -- high policy entropy ensures the independent samples span different subsets. An explicit inter-play diversity reward (e.g., Hamming distance between plays) can be added on top of the entropy bonus for additional diversification.
offline_vs_online_rl_compatibility: High offline compatibility. MaxEnt RL as a technique is orthogonal to the online/offline distinction -- it modifies the objective function but not the data collection mechanism. When layered onto an offline algorithm (e.g., CQL, IQL, or batch REINFORCE on historical draws), the entropy bonus continues to function correctly: it discourages the policy from collapsing to the actions most represented in the historical dataset. This is particularly valuable in the lottery domain where the historical dataset is fixed (one draw per week, no online interaction possible). The entropy bonus also partially mitigates distributional shift artifacts (overconfident Q-values for out-of-distribution plays) by keeping the policy from deviating too far from a diverse distribution. Fully offline-compatible without modification.
complexity: Low. MaxEnt RL is a modification of the training objective, not a new architecture. Adding an entropy bonus to an existing REINFORCE or Actor-Critic training loop requires approximately 5-15 lines of code: compute the entropy of the policy distribution at each step, multiply by alpha, subtract from the loss (or add to reward). Integrating automatic alpha tuning (dual gradient descent on a target entropy constraint) adds another 20-30 lines. The technique slots cleanly into the existing predict.py and any future actor_critic.py without structural changes to the SharedLotteryTransformer.
key_dependencies: PyTorch only (torch.distributions.Categorical.entropy() provides the exact entropy in one line). No external RL library required. Optional: torchrl for replay buffer management if combined with off-policy training.
estimated_lines_of_code: 30-80 lines total: entropy computation per step (~5 lines), entropy bonus integration into loss/reward (~10 lines), alpha hyperparameter or automatic tuning (~15-50 lines), logging of per-step entropy for diagnostics (~10 lines). If combined with an existing REINFORCE or Actor-Critic loop, the entropy bonus is a minimal add-on.
transfer_learning_compatibility: Full compatibility. MaxEnt RL is purely an objective-level modification -- it adds an entropy term to the loss function. The SharedLotteryTransformer encoder architecture, weights, and lottery_id embeddings are completely unchanged. The entropy bonus is computed from the softmax output of the existing per-lottery heads, requiring no new parameters. The pretrained swarm checkpoint (models/best_swarm.pt) can be loaded and fine-tuned with the MaxEnt objective from epoch 1, with the entropy bonus immediately active. This is the lowest-friction RL augmentation possible: zero architectural changes, zero new parameters, minimal code addition.
specific_application_in_project: MaxEnt RL is the single highest-priority Phase 2 addition because it directly fixes the documented failure mode of the current generation system. In src/predict.py (and main_swarm.py predict), the current temperature-softmax sampling can collapse to near-identical plays when temperature is low (exploitation) or generate fully random plays when temperature is high (pure exploration) -- neither gives diverse, informed predictions. Adding an entropy bonus to the REINFORCE training loop (when fine-tuning on historical draws) penalizes the policy for repeating the same number combinations. Concretely: (1) after each draw is logged via main_swarm.py log, run N gradient steps of REINFORCE where the loss = -reward * log_prob - alpha * entropy; (2) the entropy term is computed from the per-step masked softmax distribution; (3) alpha is a new hyperparameter in config.py (suggested default: 0.01-0.1); (4) plays generated by predict.py will automatically span a wider range of number combinations across calls. Applies to all three lotteries (lottomax, 649, dailygrand) via the shared encoder. This is a prerequisite for the Actor-Critic play generation in Phase 2 -- any actor-critic system should include MaxEnt regularization by default.
replaces_or_extends: Extends temperature-softmax sampling in src/predict.py -- the temperature parameter remains but is now supplemented by an entropy bonus during training rather than only controlling inference diversity. Does not replace any component; adds an entropy regularization term to the training loss in any future actor_critic.py or REINFORCE fine-tuning loop.
existing_open_source_implementations: 1. Haarnoja et al. SAC implementation (official): github.com/haarnoja/sac -- includes entropy tuning. 2. CleanRL: cleanrl/sac_continuous_action.py and sac_atari.py -- entropy coefficient auto-tuning included, clean PyTorch. 3. Stable-Baselines3: SAC and TQC implementations include automatic entropy tuning for continuous spaces. 4. torchrl (Meta/PyTorch): SACLoss class includes entropy computation. 5. PyTorch built-in: torch.distributions.Categorical.entropy() returns exact entropy for discrete policies in one call, making custom implementation trivial. 6. OpenAI Spinning Up: spinningup/algos/pytorch/sac/ -- clean entropy-regularized actor-critic reference.
benchmark_results: Haarnoja et al. (2018): SAC (MaxEnt RL + off-policy) outperforms PPO, DDPG, and TD3 on MuJoCo continuous control tasks in both final performance and sample efficiency, with entropy regularization credited for preventing premature convergence. Ziebart et al. (2010): MaxEnt IRL outperforms max-margin IRL on taxi route prediction with ~200 expert trajectories, demonstrating robustness on small demonstration datasets. Christodoulou (2019): SAC-Discrete with entropy regularization matches DQN on Atari with fewer environment steps. No published benchmarks directly on combinatorial discrete action spaces with N=50, k=7 or lottery-style prediction. The entropy bonus's effect on play diversity is deterministic by construction (higher alpha = higher entropy = more diverse plays) and does not require empirical validation for this specific property.
notable_use_cases: 1. Robot locomotion (SAC with entropy bonus prevents gait collapse on sparse terrain rewards -- directly analogous to play collapse). 2. Inverse RL for human trajectory prediction (Ziebart 2010, ~200-500 demonstrations, structurally similar to 100-200 draw history). 3. Recommendation systems with entropy regularization to prevent filter bubble collapse -- selects k items from N candidates, sparse implicit feedback, mirrors the lottery structure. 4. Molecular generation with MaxEnt RL (select atom types sequentially from a discrete pool, sparse reward from docking score -- combinatorial discrete output with sparse reward, very similar to lottery number selection). 5. Text generation with entropy-regularized language models (prevents output collapse to repetitive phrases -- same collapse phenomenon as repeated lottery plays).
